q: The opening stock of a material is 300 units at Rs 14 per unit. A further 200 units are purchased at Rs 18 per unit. If 250 units are issued to production, the value of the issue under the LIFO method is:
e: Under LIFO the latest purchases are issued first: 200 units at Rs 18 = Rs 3,600 plus 50 units from opening stock at Rs 14 = Rs 700, giving Rs 4,300 for 250 units.

q: Under the integral system of accounting:

options.A: Separate cost and financial ledgers are maintained and their results are reconciled
options.B: Only financial accounts are maintained and cost figures are taken from them
options.C: Cost accounts and financial accounts are combined in a single set of books, so that no reconciliation between the two is necessary
options.D: Cost accounts are maintained only for finished products

e: Under the integral system cost and financial accounts are kept in one combined set of books, so both results come from the same records and no reconciliation between separate ledgers is needed.

q: Under Barth's variable sharing plan of wage payment, a worker's earnings are computed as the hourly wage rate multiplied by the geometric mean (square root of the product) of the standard hours and the actual hours taken. A worker is allowed 100 hours for a job, completes it in 64 hours and is paid at Rs 10 per hour. His total earnings are:
e: Barth earnings = rate x sqrt(standard hours x actual hours) = Rs 10 x sqrt(100 x 64) = Rs 10 x 80 = Rs 800, rewarding the worker increasingly as time saved grows.

q: In the primary distribution of factory overheads, the expenses of lighting and heating of the factory are usually apportioned among the departments on the basis of:

options.A: The number of workers employed in each department
options.B: The number of light points (or wattage) in each department
options.C: The direct wages paid in each department
options.D: The value of plant and machinery in each department

e: Lighting and heating serve the space occupied, best measured by the number of light points or wattage in each department, so primary distribution apportions these expenses on that basis.

q: The re-order level of a material is 3,600 units and the re-order quantity is 2,400 units. The minimum consumption is 250 units per week and the minimum delivery period is 4 weeks. The maximum stock level of the material is:
e: Maximum stock level = re-order level + re-order quantity - (minimum consumption x minimum delivery period) = 3,600 + 2,400 - (250 x 4) = 5,000 units.

q: Job costing is the most suitable method of costing for:

options.C: A printing press executing specific orders of customers

e: Job costing suits work done against specific customer orders, each job being separately costed; a printing press executing individual orders is the classic case, unlike continuous-process industries.

q: Under Gantt's task and bonus plan, a worker who completes his task within the standard time is paid time wages plus a bonus of 20% of the time wages. A worker is allowed 10 hours for a job, completes it in 8 hours and is paid at Rs 50 per hour. His total earnings are:
e: The task is finished within standard time, so Gantt pays time wages plus 20% bonus: wages for 8 hours x Rs 50 = Rs 400, bonus Rs 80, total Rs 480.

q: In contract accounts, work which has been done but has not yet been certified by the engineer or architect is shown as work uncertified, and it is valued at:

options.C: The value certified for similar work

e: Work done but not yet certified cannot be billed, so in contract accounts work uncertified is valued conservatively at cost price, not at contract price or certified value.

q: Budgeted factory overheads of a concern are Rs 5,00,000 and the budgeted direct labour hours are 40,000, giving a predetermined absorption rate. Actual direct labour hours worked are 38,000 and the actual factory overheads incurred are Rs 5,10,000. The overheads are:
e: Absorption rate = Rs 5,00,000 / 40,000 hours = Rs 12.50 per hour. Absorbed = 38,000 x Rs 12.50 = Rs 4,75,000; actual Rs 5,10,000, so overheads are under-absorbed by Rs 35,000.

q: A 'basic standard' in standard costing is a standard which:

options.A: Is established for use over a long period, remains unaltered despite changed conditions, and serves mainly as a basis for measuring the trend of efficiency
options.B: Is revised at the beginning of every accounting period
options.C: Represents the level of efficiency currently attainable under normal conditions
options.D: Is set at the maximum level of efficiency theoretically possible

e: A basic standard is set once for a long period and left unchanged whatever conditions become; it is not a target for current efficiency but a base for measuring long-run efficiency trends.

q: Fixed production overheads of a factory are Rs 1,50,000. Production during the period is 25,000 units and sales are 22,000 units. Compared with marginal costing, the profit under absorption costing for the period will be:
e: Fixed overhead rate = Rs 1,50,000 / 25,000 units = Rs 6 per unit. Unsold stock of 3,000 units carries 3,000 x Rs 6 = Rs 18,000 into stock under absorption costing, so its profit is higher by Rs 18,000.

q: In activity-based costing, 'customer-level' (customer-sustaining) activities are activities which:

options.A: Are performed for each unit of product manufactured
options.B: Are performed for each batch of products processed
options.C: Make it possible to sell the products of the concern in general
options.D: Are performed to support individual customers, irrespective of the number of units or batches supplied to them

e: Customer-level activities support a particular customer regardless of how many units or batches he takes - for example dedicated account management - so their cost is traced to customers, not products.

q: A product sells for Rs 210 per unit and its variable cost is Rs 126 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 3,00,000 and 4,500 units are sold. The profit under marginal costing is:
e: Profit = contribution - fixed costs = (Rs 210 - Rs 126) x 4,500 - Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 3,78,000 - Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 78,000 under marginal costing.

q: The cost of secondary packing of a product — such as cartons and crates used for packing the finished goods for transport and display — is treated in cost accounts as:

options.B: A part of the prime cost of the product

e: Secondary packing (cartons, crates) protects and presents finished goods for transport and display after production is complete, so it is a selling and distribution overhead, not a production cost.

q: A product sells for Rs 450 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 270 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 14,40,000. The break-even point in units is:
e: Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution per unit = Rs 14,40,000 / (Rs 450 - Rs 270) = Rs 14,40,000 / Rs 180 = 8,000 units.

q: 'Inter-firm comparison' is a technique under which:

options.A: The costs of two departments of the same firm are compared with each other
options.B: Firms in the same industry pool uniform cost and performance data so that each firm can compare its efficiency with the industry average
options.C: The cost of a product is compared with its selling price
options.D: The actual cost of a firm is compared with its standard cost

e: Inter-firm comparison pools uniform costing data from firms in the same industry through a common scheme, letting each firm benchmark its costs and efficiency against the industry average.

q: An enterprise records the following: Sales Rs 4,00,000 with profit Rs 20,000 in Year 1, and Sales Rs 6,00,000 with profit Rs 80,000 in Year 2. The P/V ratio is:
e: P/V ratio = change in profit / change in sales = (Rs 80,000 - Rs 20,000) / (Rs 6,00,000 - Rs 4,00,000) = Rs 60,000 / Rs 2,00,000 = 30%.

q: An 'escalation clause' in a contract provides for:

options.A: Adjustment of the contract price in the event of changes in the prices of materials, rates of wages and similar factors during the execution of the contract
options.B: Extension of the period allowed for completion of the contract
options.C: Payment of the contract price in instalments as the work progresses
options.D: Termination of the contract by either party on notice

e: An escalation clause lets the contract price be adjusted for changes in material prices, wage rates and similar factors during execution, protecting both parties on long-duration contracts.

q: Machine hours are the limiting factor in a factory. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 105 per unit and requires 7 machine hours per unit; Product B gives a contribution of Rs 132 per unit and requires 6 machine hours per unit. Production priority should be given to:

options.D: Neither product, as their contributions per unit are nearly equal

e: Contribution per machine hour (the limiting factor): A = Rs 105 / 7 = Rs 15; B = Rs 132 / 6 = Rs 22. B yields more per scarce hour, so B gets priority.

q: Under the direct allocation method of secondary distribution of overheads:

options.A: The costs of each service department are distributed to the other service departments and production departments in turn
options.B: The costs of service departments are apportioned by solving simultaneous equations
options.C: The costs of service departments are repeatedly redistributed until the amounts become negligible
options.D: The costs of service departments are apportioned only to the production departments, ignoring the services rendered by one service department to another

e: Under direct allocation, service department costs are apportioned straight to production departments only; services one service department renders to another are ignored, unlike the step, simultaneous-equation or repeated-distribution methods.

q: A factory has 18,000 machine hours available. Product A, which ranks first on the basis of contribution per machine hour, requires 6 machine hours per unit and its maximum demand is 2,000 units. Product B requires 4 machine hours per unit. After meeting the full demand for A, the number of units of B that can be produced is:
e: Hours used by A = 2,000 units x 6 = 12,000 hours. Hours left = 18,000 - 12,000 = 6,000; units of B = 6,000 / 4 = 1,500 units.

q: Materials destroyed by an accidental fire in a factory represent an abnormal loss. In cost accounts, the value of such materials is:

options.A: Excluded from the cost of production and debited to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.B: Treated as a part of the factory overheads of the period
options.C: Added to the cost of the goods produced during the period
options.D: Charged to the administration overheads of the concern

e: Loss by accidental fire is abnormal, not a normal cost of production, so its value is excluded from production cost and debited to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: A component can be made in the factory at a variable cost of Rs 42 per unit, or bought from an outside supplier at Rs 47 per unit. If the component is bought, the capacity released can be used to earn a contribution of Rs 8 per unit on other work. All fixed costs will continue in either case. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Make the component, as its variable cost of Rs 42 is less than the purchase price of Rs 47
options.B: Buy the component, as its effective cost, after crediting the contribution of Rs 8, is Rs 39 per unit
options.C: Make the component, as buying would cost Rs 8 per unit more
options.D: Remain indifferent, as both alternatives cost the same

e: Buying frees capacity earning Rs 8 per unit, so the effective cost of buying = Rs 47 - Rs 8 = Rs 39 per unit, below the Rs 42 cost of making; buying is cheaper.

q: During a period of continuously falling prices of materials, the LIFO method of pricing issues, as compared with the FIFO method, results in:

options.A: A higher cost of production and a lower value of closing stock
options.B: A higher value of closing stock and a higher cost of production
options.C: A lower cost of production and a higher value of closing stock
options.D: No difference in either the cost of production or the value of closing stock

e: With prices falling, LIFO charges the latest (cheaper) purchases to production, giving a lower cost of production, while closing stock keeps the older (costlier) layers, giving it a higher value than under FIFO.

q: A firm has spare capacity. Its variable cost is Rs 52 per unit. It receives a one-time special order for 6,000 units at Rs 58 per unit, but accepting the order requires additional fixed expenditure of Rs 24,000. The order should be:

options.A: Rejected, as it would result in a loss of Rs 12,000
options.B: Accepted, as it would increase the profit by Rs 36,000
options.C: Rejected, as the price is below the total cost per unit
options.D: Accepted, as it would increase the profit by Rs 12,000

e: Extra contribution = (Rs 58 - Rs 52) x 6,000 = Rs 36,000; less additional fixed cost Rs 24,000 gives a profit increase of Rs 12,000, so with spare capacity the order should be accepted.

q: The Economic Batch Quantity (EBQ) in batch costing is the batch size at which:

options.A: The total of the set-up (preparation) costs and the carrying (holding) costs of the batch is the minimum
options.B: The set-up cost per batch is the minimum
options.C: The carrying cost of the batch is nil
options.D: The production cost per unit is equal to its selling price

e: The Economic Batch Quantity balances the two opposing costs of batch production - set-up cost per batch against carrying cost of the batch - and is the size minimising their total.

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 4,50,000 per year, of which Rs 1,80,000 would continue to be incurred even during a shutdown. Shutdown (discontinuance) costs of Rs 30,000 would also be incurred if the plant is closed. The contribution is Rs 25 per unit. The shutdown point of the plant is:
e: Shutdown point = (avoidable fixed costs + shutdown costs) / contribution per unit = ((Rs 4,50,000 - Rs 1,80,000) + Rs 30,000) / Rs 25 = Rs 3,00,000 / Rs 25 = 12,000 units. Below this, shutting down loses less.

q: Break-even (CVP) analysis rests on a number of assumptions. Which of the following is one of them?

options.A: The selling price per unit varies with the level of sales
options.B: Total fixed costs increase in proportion to the output
options.C: The selling price per unit and the variable cost per unit remain constant at all levels of activity
options.D: All costs are treated as fixed costs

e: Break-even analysis assumes linearity: selling price per unit and variable cost per unit stay constant, and total fixed cost stays fixed, at all activity levels within the relevant range.

q: A division earns a contribution of Rs 1,75,000. Its specific (avoidable) fixed costs are Rs 1,50,000, besides which common fixed costs of Rs 70,000 are allocated to it and would continue even if the division were closed. If the division is closed down, the total profit of the company will:
e: Closing the division loses its contribution of Rs 1,75,000 but saves only its avoidable fixed costs of Rs 1,50,000 (common costs continue), so company profit falls by Rs 25,000; the division should be kept.

q: In operating costing, the cost unit commonly used for a boiler house is:
e: A boiler house produces steam, so its operating cost is expressed per kilogram (or tonne) of steam generated - the natural cost unit for that service.

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 28 per kg and the actual price paid is Rs 26 per kg. The actual quantity consumed is 2,500 kg. The material price variance is:
e: Material price variance = (standard price - actual price) x actual quantity = (Rs 28 - Rs 26) x 2,500 kg = Rs 5,000 Favourable, since the actual price is lower.

q: For the actual output, the standard material cost is 900 kg at Rs 24 per kg. The actual consumption is 950 kg purchased at Rs 26 per kg. The material cost variance is:
e: Material cost variance = standard cost - actual cost = (900 x Rs 24) - (950 x Rs 26) = Rs 21,600 - Rs 24,700 = Rs 3,100 Adverse.

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time is 2,200 hours, but only 2,050 hours were actually taken. The standard wage rate is Rs 44 per hour. The labour efficiency variance is:
e: Labour efficiency variance = (standard hours - actual hours) x standard rate = (2,200 - 2,050) x Rs 44 = 150 x Rs 44 = Rs 6,600 Favourable, as less time was taken.

q: The budgeted sales of a product are 6,000 units and the actual sales are 5,400 units. The standard profit margin is Rs 25 per unit. The sales margin volume variance is:
e: Sales margin volume variance = (actual sales - budgeted sales) x standard profit per unit = (5,400 - 6,000) x Rs 25 = Rs 15,000 Adverse, because 600 fewer units were sold.

q: In a process, 8,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 1,53,600. Normal loss is 10% of the input and the scrap realises Rs 12 per unit. The cost per unit of good output is:
e: Cost per unit = (total cost - scrap value of normal loss) / expected good output = (Rs 1,53,600 - 800 x Rs 12) / 7,200 = Rs 1,44,000 / 7,200 = Rs 20.

q: In a process, 4,500 units are introduced and the normal loss is 10% of the input. The actual output obtained is 4,140 units. The difference is:
e: Expected output = 4,500 - 10% normal loss = 4,050 units. Actual output 4,140 exceeds this by 90 units, so there is an abnormal gain of 90 units.

q: In a process, 7,000 units were completed and transferred to the next process during a period. The closing work-in-progress is 1,500 units, which are 40% complete in respect of conversion costs, and there was no opening work-in-progress. The equivalent production in respect of conversion costs is:
e: Equivalent production for conversion = completed units + (closing WIP x degree of completion) = 7,000 + (1,500 x 40%) = 7,000 + 600 = 7,600 units.

q: A joint product can be sold at the split-off point for Rs 45 per unit. It can alternatively be processed further at an additional cost of Rs 18 per unit and then sold for Rs 58 per unit. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Process it further, as it gives a gain of Rs 13 per unit
options.B: Process it further, as it gives a gain of Rs 18 per unit
options.C: Remain indifferent between the two alternatives
options.D: Sell it at the split-off point, as further processing would reduce the profit by Rs 5 per unit

e: Further processing adds revenue of Rs 58 - Rs 45 = Rs 13 per unit but costs Rs 18, a net loss of Rs 5 per unit, so the product should be sold at the split-off point.

q: Under activity-based costing, the quality testing cost pool of a plant is Rs 4,20,000 and the total number of tests performed in the period is 2,100. A product which requires 350 tests will be assigned quality testing cost of:
e: Cost driver rate = Rs 4,20,000 / 2,100 tests = Rs 200 per test. Cost assigned = 350 tests x Rs 200 = Rs 70,000.

q: The budgeted production of a factory is 30,000 units and the standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 6 per unit. Actual production is 26,000 units. The fixed overhead volume variance is:
e: Fixed overhead volume variance = (actual production - budgeted production) x standard rate = (26,000 - 30,000) x Rs 6 = Rs 24,000 Adverse, because output fell short of budget.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 5,50,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 2,20,000 at the end of each of the next 4 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 15% is 2.855. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: NPV = (Rs 2,20,000 x 2.855) - Rs 5,50,000 = Rs 6,28,100 - Rs 5,50,000 = (+) Rs 78,100, so the project earns more than the 15% required return.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 9,50,000. Its net cash inflows are Rs 4,00,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor at 12% = 0.893), Rs 4,00,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor at 12% = 0.797) and Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 3 (present value factor at 12% = 0.712). The Net Present Value of the project is:
The present value of Rs 5,00,000 receivable at the end of 5 years, discounted at 10% (present value factor 0.621), is:
e: Present value = Rs 5,00,000 x 0.621 = Rs 3,10,500, the amount worth paying today for Rs 5,00,000 receivable after 5 years at 10%.

q: Rs 2,50,000 invested today at 12% per annum compound interest will grow in 2 years to (the compound value factor for 2 years at 12% is 1.254):
e: Future value = Rs 2,50,000 x 1.254 = Rs 3,13,500 after 2 years at 12% compound interest.

q: A machine costing Rs 14,40,000 generates a net cash inflow of Rs 2,40,000 per year. Its payback period is:
e: Payback period = initial outlay / annual cash inflow = Rs 14,40,000 / Rs 2,40,000 = 6 years, since the inflow is uniform each year.

q: A project costing Rs 7,50,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 2,00,000 in Year 1, Rs 2,50,000 in Year 2, Rs 2,00,000 in Year 3 and Rs 1,50,000 in Year 4. Its payback period is:
e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 Rs 2,00,000, Year 2 Rs 4,50,000, Year 3 Rs 6,50,000. Balance Rs 1,00,000 comes from Year 4 inflow of Rs 1,50,000, taking 8 months, so payback is 3 years 8 months.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 4,20,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 2,40,000 at the end of Year 1 and Rs 2,40,000 at the end of Year 2. The discounted payback period of the project is:
e: By end of Year 1, Rs 2,40,000 of the Rs 4,20,000 outlay is recovered in present-value terms; the remaining Rs 1,80,000 takes Rs 1,80,000 / Rs 2,40,000 = 0.75 year = 9 months, so discounted payback is 1 year 9 months.

q: A project's Net Present Value is (+) Rs 15,000 at a discount rate of 12% and (-) Rs 10,000 at a discount rate of 16%. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
e: IRR = 12% + (15,000 / (15,000 + 10,000)) x (16% - 12%) = 12% + 0.6 x 4% = 14.4%, interpolating between the positive and negative NPVs.

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 7,20,000 and its initial investment is Rs 9,00,000. The Profitability Index of the project is:
e: Profitability Index = present value of inflows / initial investment = Rs 7,20,000 / Rs 9,00,000 = 0.80. Being below 1, it confirms the project's NPV is negative.

q: An investment of Rs 15,00,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit after depreciation and tax of Rs 1,05,000. The Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: Average Rate of Return = average annual profit / initial investment x 100 = Rs 1,05,000 / Rs 15,00,000 x 100 = 7%.

q: An investment of Rs 12,50,000 has an expected salvage value of Rs 2,50,000 at the end of its life, so that the average investment over its life is Rs 7,50,000. If the average annual profit after depreciation and tax is Rs 1,35,000, the Average Rate of Return computed on the average investment is:
e: ARR on average investment = average annual profit / average investment x 100 = Rs 1,35,000 / Rs 7,50,000 x 100 = 18%. Average investment is (Rs 12,50,000 + Rs 2,50,000) / 2.

q: In the NPV profile of a project (a graph of the project's net present value plotted against different discount rates), the point at which the NPV curve cuts the discount-rate axis represents the project's:
e: The NPV profile plots NPV against the discount rate; where the curve crosses the discount-rate (horizontal) axis, NPV is zero, and that rate is by definition the internal rate of return.

q: A company's capital structure consists of equity capital of Rs 20,00,000 (cost 13%), preference capital of Rs 5,00,000 (cost 10%) and debt of Rs 15,00,000 (after-tax cost 6%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company's capital structure consists of debt of Rs 12,00,000 with an after-tax cost of 7% and equity of Rs 28,00,000 with a cost of 15%. Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company issues 12% debentures of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 90 per debenture. Ignoring tax and redemption premium, the cost of debt is:
e: Cost of debt = annual interest / net proceeds per debenture = Rs 12 / Rs 90 = 13.33%, because the debentures were issued at a discount of Rs 10.

q: A company issues 11% preference shares of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 110 per share. The cost of preference capital is:
e: Cost of preference capital = preference dividend / issue price = Rs 11 / Rs 110 = 10%, the dividend being measured against what the company actually received per share.

q: A share is expected to pay a dividend of Rs 9 per share next year. Its market price is Rs 72 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 4% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity = (expected dividend / market price) + growth rate = (Rs 9 / Rs 72) + 4% = 12.5% + 4% = 16.5% under the dividend growth model.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the risk-free rate is 8%, the expected market return is 14% and the beta of the share is 1.1, the cost of equity is:
e: CAPM cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta x (market return - risk-free rate) = 8% + 1.1 x (14% - 8%) = 8% + 6.6% = 14.6%.

q: The cost of debt capital is generally lower than the cost of equity capital mainly because:

options.A: Lenders have a prior and fixed claim on earnings and assets and bear less risk, and interest payable to them is deductible as an expense for tax purposes, unlike dividends
options.B: Debentures are always issued at a discount to their face value
options.C: Equity shares have a fixed date of maturity, unlike debentures
options.D: Debenture holders are given voting rights in the company

e: Debt is cheaper because lenders have a prior, fixed claim and bear less risk than shareholders, and interest is tax-deductible whereas dividends are paid out of after-tax profits.

q: Under the Modigliani-Miller hypothesis (when taxes are ignored), if two firms which are identical in all respects except their capital structures have different total market values, investors can earn a riskless profit by selling the shares of the over-valued firm and purchasing shares of the under-valued firm, thereby bringing the values into line. This process is known as:
e: This buying-and-selling between identical firms to exploit a valuation gap, until arbitrage forces the two total values into line, is the arbitrage process underlying the Modigliani-Miller hypothesis.

q: The 'bird-in-hand' theory of dividend policy, associated with Gordon and Lintner, argues that:

options.A: The value of a firm is independent of its dividend policy
options.B: Investors, being risk-averse, prefer a dividend in hand (which is certain) to prospective capital gains (which are uncertain), so a higher dividend payout tends to lower the cost of equity
options.C: Dividends should be paid only out of the earnings left after meeting all investment needs
options.D: A higher dividend payout raises the cost of equity of the firm

e: Gordon and Lintner's bird-in-hand theory holds that risk-averse investors value a certain current dividend more than uncertain future capital gains, so a higher payout lowers the cost of equity and raises value.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 40,00,000, variable costs are Rs 26,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 6,00,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
e: Degree of operating leverage = contribution / EBIT = (Rs 40,00,000 - Rs 26,00,000) / (Rs 14,00,000 - Rs 6,00,000) = Rs 14,00,000 / Rs 8,00,000 = 1.75.

q: An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 15,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 6,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT / (EBIT - interest) = Rs 15,00,000 / (Rs 15,00,000 - Rs 6,00,000) = Rs 15,00,000 / Rs 9,00,000 = 1.67.

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 36,00,000, variable costs of Rs 20,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 6,00,000 and interest of Rs 2,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Degree of combined leverage = contribution / (contribution - fixed costs - interest) = Rs 16,00,000 / (Rs 16,00,000 - Rs 6,00,000 - Rs 2,00,000) = Rs 16,00,000 / Rs 8,00,000 = 2.0.

q: The degree of operating leverage of an enterprise is 3.2. If its sales increase by 10%, its earnings before interest and tax will increase by approximately:
e: Percentage change in EBIT = degree of operating leverage x percentage change in sales = 3.2 x 10% = 32%, since operating leverage magnifies the effect of sales changes on operating profit.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 17,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 10,00,000. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = Rs 17,00,000 / Rs 10,00,000 = 1.7 : 1.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 9,60,000, comprising stock of Rs 3,60,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 60,000. Current liabilities are Rs 3,00,000. The quick (acid-test) ratio is:
e: Quick assets = current assets - stock - prepaid expenses = Rs 9,60,000 - Rs 3,60,000 - Rs 60,000 = Rs 5,40,000. Quick ratio = Rs 5,40,000 / Rs 3,00,000 = 1.8 : 1.

q: Long-term debt of an enterprise is Rs 11,00,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 5,50,000. The debt-equity ratio is:
e: Debt-equity ratio = long-term debt / shareholders' funds = Rs 11,00,000 / Rs 5,50,000 = 2 : 1.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 28,00,000 and the cost of goods sold is Rs 19,60,000. Its gross profit ratio is:
e: Gross profit ratio = (sales - cost of goods sold) / sales x 100 = (Rs 28,00,000 - Rs 19,60,000) / Rs 28,00,000 x 100 = Rs 8,40,000 / Rs 28,00,000 = 30%.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 1,95,000 on sales of Rs 15,00,000. Its net profit ratio is:
e: Net profit ratio = net profit / sales x 100 = Rs 1,95,000 / Rs 15,00,000 x 100 = 13%.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 27,00,000 and its average inventory is Rs 3,00,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
e: Inventory turnover ratio = cost of goods sold / average inventory = Rs 27,00,000 / Rs 3,00,000 = 9 times, showing stock is sold and replaced nine times a year.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 19,20,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,60,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover ratio = credit sales / average debtors = Rs 19,20,000 / Rs 1,60,000 = 12 times.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 18,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 3,00,000. Taking a year of 360 days, the average collection period is:
e: Average collection period = average debtors / credit sales x 360 = Rs 3,00,000 / Rs 18,00,000 x 360 = 60 days.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 9,60,000 and the interest payable is Rs 1,20,000. The interest coverage ratio is:
e: Interest coverage ratio = profit before interest and tax / interest = Rs 9,60,000 / Rs 1,20,000 = 8 times, showing earnings cover the interest charge eight times over.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 10,50,000 and its capital employed is Rs 25,00,000. The Return on Capital Employed is:
e: Return on Capital Employed = profit before interest and tax / capital employed x 100 = Rs 10,50,000 / Rs 25,00,000 x 100 = 42%.

q: The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 12,00,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 2,00,000. If the company has 4,00,000 equity shares, its Earnings Per Share (EPS) is:
e: EPS = (net profit after tax - preference dividend) / number of equity shares = (Rs 12,00,000 - Rs 2,00,000) / 4,00,000 = Rs 2.50 per share.

q: The market price of a company's share is Rs 64 and its Earnings Per Share is Rs 4. The price-earnings (P/E) ratio is:
e: Price-earnings ratio = market price per share / earnings per share = Rs 64 / Rs 4 = 16, meaning investors pay sixteen times the annual earnings for the share.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 6,00,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 70,000 and a loss of Rs 12,000 on the sale of investments, and after crediting a profit of Rs 40,000 on the sale of plant. The funds from operations are:
e: Funds from operations = Rs 6,00,000 + depreciation Rs 70,000 + loss on sale of investments Rs 12,000 - profit on sale of plant Rs 40,000 = Rs 6,42,000; non-fund items are added back or removed.

q: An enterprise's operating profit before working capital changes is Rs 4,80,000. During the year, its stock decreased by Rs 30,000, its debtors increased by Rs 60,000 and its creditors increased by Rs 10,000. The cash from operations is:
e: Cash from operations = Rs 4,80,000 + stock decrease Rs 30,000 - debtors increase Rs 60,000 + creditors increase Rs 10,000 = Rs 4,60,000. A fall in stock releases cash; a rise in debtors absorbs it.

q: During a year, the current assets of an enterprise increased by Rs 2,50,000 and its current liabilities increased by Rs 1,50,000. The net change in its working capital is:
e: Change in working capital = increase in current assets - increase in current liabilities = Rs 2,50,000 - Rs 1,50,000 = an increase of Rs 1,00,000.

q: In a cash flow statement prepared under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), the interest received by a non-financial enterprise on its investments and loans is classified as a:

options.D: It is not shown in the cash flow statement at all

e: Under AS-3, for a non-financial enterprise interest received on investments and loans arises from deploying funds in assets, so it is an investing activity; only financial enterprises treat it as operating.

q: The net earnings of a railway are Rs 15,300 crore and its capital-at-charge is Rs 1,80,000 crore. The return on capital-at-charge is:
e: Return on capital-at-charge = net earnings / capital-at-charge x 100 = Rs 15,300 crore / Rs 1,80,000 crore x 100 = 8.5%, the Railways' measure of earnings on capital invested.

q: A railway earned gross traffic receipts of Rs 5,00,000 crore against ordinary working expenses of Rs 4,85,000 crore. Its Operating Ratio is:
e: Operating Ratio = ordinary working expenses / gross traffic receipts x 100 = Rs 4,85,000 crore / Rs 5,00,000 crore x 100 = 97%, meaning 97 paise are spent to earn each rupee.

q: A proposed railway work is estimated to cost Rs 600 crore and is expected to yield net annual earnings of Rs 57 crore after meeting the additional working expenses. The anticipated rate of return on the work, and its financial status, are:

options.A: 9.5%, and the work is financially remunerative
options.B: 10.5%, and the work is financially remunerative
options.C: 9.5%, and the work passes the test because any return above 9% is acceptable
options.D: 9.5%, and the work is unremunerative as it falls short of the prescribed 10% test of remunerativeness

e: Rate of return = Rs 57 crore / Rs 600 crore x 100 = 9.5%. Railway works must clear the prescribed 10% test of remunerativeness, so at 9.5% the work is unremunerative.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Financial Internal Rate of Return (FIRR) of a railway project is computed from the point of view of the Railways, taking into account only the financial earnings and financial costs of the project.
2. The Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) of a project is computed from the point of view of the economy as a whole, taking into account the social benefits and social costs of the project.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
e: Both statements are correct: FIRR judges the project purely on the Railways' own financial earnings and costs, while EIRR judges it for the economy as a whole using social benefits and social costs.

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 72,000 units. The opening stock of finished goods is 9,000 units and the closing stock is to be 12,000 units. The production budget should provide for production of:
e: Production budget = budgeted sales + closing stock - opening stock = 72,000 + 12,000 - 9,000 = 75,000 units.

q: Production of 28,000 units is budgeted, each unit requiring 3 kg of material. The opening stock of material is 10,000 kg and the closing stock is to be 13,000 kg. The quantity of material to be purchased is:
e: Material to be purchased = production requirement + closing stock - opening stock = (28,000 x 3) + 13,000 - 10,000 = 84,000 + 3,000 = 87,000 kg.

q: A cash budget shows an opening cash balance of Rs 55,000, estimated receipts of Rs 3,75,000 and estimated payments of Rs 3,95,000 for a month. The closing cash balance will be:
e: Closing cash balance = opening balance + receipts - payments = Rs 55,000 + Rs 3,75,000 - Rs 3,95,000 = Rs 35,000.

q: An enterprise pays for its credit purchases 40% in the month of purchase and the remaining 60% in the following month. Purchases were Rs 1,20,000 in the previous month and are budgeted at Rs 1,50,000 in the current month. The cash payment for purchases in the current month will be:
e: Payment for purchases = 40% of current month's purchases + 60% of previous month's = (40% x Rs 1,50,000) + (60% x Rs 1,20,000) = Rs 60,000 + Rs 72,000 = Rs 1,32,000.

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 2,70,000 and variable costs of Rs 16 per unit. The total flexed budget allowance for an actual output of 22,000 units is:
e: Flexed budget allowance = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit x actual output) = Rs 2,70,000 + (Rs 16 x 22,000) = Rs 2,70,000 + Rs 3,52,000 = Rs 6,22,000.

q: A forecast differs from a budget mainly in that:

options.A: A forecast is prepared by the accounts department, whereas a budget is prepared by the sales department
options.B: A forecast is an estimate of what is likely to happen, whereas a budget is a formal plan of what management intends to achieve, serving as a target and a standard for control
options.C: A forecast covers a short period, whereas a budget always covers five years
options.D: There is no difference between the two

e: A forecast merely estimates what is likely to happen; a budget is a formal, approved plan of intended action expressed in figures, used as a target and as a standard for controlling performance.

q: Under the adjusted profit and loss (cash flow) method of preparing a cash budget, the starting point is:

options.A: The opening cash balance of the period
options.B: The total credit sales of the period
options.C: The budgeted balance sheet of the previous year
options.D: The budgeted net profit for the period, which is then adjusted for non-cash items such as depreciation and for changes in working capital and capital items to arrive at the expected cash position

e: The adjusted profit and loss method starts from the budgeted net profit and adjusts it for non-cash items like depreciation, working-capital changes and capital receipts and payments to reach the expected cash balance.

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 28 days, the production process takes 14 days, finished goods are held for 24 days and debtors take 44 days to pay. Suppliers allow 26 days' credit. The length of the operating cycle is:
e: Operating cycle = raw materials 28 + production 14 + finished goods 24 + debtors 44 - creditors 26 = 84 days.

q: The annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 50,40,000 (reckoning a year of 360 days). Its operating cycle is 45 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
e: Working capital = annual operating cost / 360 x cycle days = Rs 50,40,000 / 360 x 45 = Rs 14,000 x 45 = Rs 6,30,000.

q: An enterprise has an inventory conversion period of 65 days, a receivables collection period of 38 days and a payables deferral period of 48 days. Its cash conversion cycle is:
e: Cash conversion cycle = inventory period + receivables period - payables period = 65 + 38 - 48 = 55 days.

q: Under the Tandon Committee's Method I of lending, the maximum permissible bank finance is 75% of the working capital gap (total current assets minus current liabilities other than bank borrowings). For a borrower with total current assets of Rs 24,00,000 and current liabilities (other than bank borrowings) of Rs 6,00,000, the maximum permissible bank finance is:
e: Working capital gap = Rs 24,00,000 - Rs 6,00,000 = Rs 18,00,000. Maximum permissible bank finance under Tandon Method I = 75% x Rs 18,00,000 = Rs 13,50,000.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 520 units per week and the maximum re-order period is 4 weeks. The re-order level for the material is:
e: Re-order level = maximum consumption x maximum re-order period = 520 units x 4 weeks = 2,080 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 3,600 units. Normal consumption is 260 units per week and the normal re-order period is 6 weeks. The minimum stock level is:
e: Minimum stock level = re-order level - (normal consumption x normal re-order period) = 3,600 - (260 x 6) = 3,600 - 1,560 = 2,040 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 3,900 units and the re-order quantity is 2,600 units. Minimum consumption is 140 units per week and the minimum re-order period is 5 weeks. The maximum stock level is:
e: Maximum stock level = re-order level + re-order quantity - (minimum consumption x minimum re-order period) = 3,900 + 2,600 - (140 x 5) = 5,800 units.

q: The maximum stock level of a material is 6,400 units and the minimum stock level is 2,400 units. The average stock level, computed as (Maximum level + Minimum level) / 2, is:
e: Average stock level = (maximum level + minimum level) / 2 = (6,400 + 2,400) / 2 = 4,400 units.
